tracks.summary: Toyota-owned circuit beneath Mount Fuji with a very long main straight; hosted the Japanese Grand Prix and a round of the World Endurance Championship.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Fuji Speedway opened in 1966 on the eastern foothills of Mount Fuji in Shizuoka Prefecture. It was originally conceived as a high-banked American-style superspeedway, but funding shortfalls meant only part of that plan was built, and the venue opened instead as a road course incorporating one steeply banked curve. That banking, blamed for several serious accidents, was later bypassed and removed. Toyota, long associated with the track, took majority ownership in 2000 and commissioned a Hermann Tilke redesign that reopened in 2005.

## The circuit
The modern lap runs 4.563 km through 16 corners and is dominated by a main straight of roughly 1.475 km, among the longest in world motorsport, which produces high top speeds and heavy braking into the first corner. The opening sector is very fast, giving way to a tighter, more technical infield in the second half of the lap. The setting beneath Mount Fuji is a distinctive feature of the venue, though the mountain itself is frequently obscured by cloud.

## Racing at Fuji
Fuji hosted the Formula One Japanese Grand Prix in 1976 and 1977, the 1976 event settling the world championship in heavy rain, after which the sport left Japan for a decade. It returned to Fuji in 2007 and 2008 before the grand prix reverted to Suzuka. The circuit's principal international fixture is now the 6 Hours of Fuji, a round of the FIA World Endurance Championship held there from 2012 to 2019 and again since 2022, and confirmed on the 2026 schedule. Fuji also anchors Japan's domestic Super GT and Super Formula seasons.

tracks.name: Mobility Resort Motegi (Twin Ring Motegi)
tracks.summary: The Japanese circuit at Motegi (renamed Mobility Resort Motegi in 2022), a technical stop-and-go road course that hosts the Japanese motorcycle Grand Prix. Its separate superspeedway oval — which held the IndyCar Indy Japan 300 from 1998 to 2011 — has since been decommissioned.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The venue was built by Honda and opened in 1997 as Twin Ring Motegi, a name that captured its unusual dual layout: a road course and a separate American-style oval superspeedway sharing one site north-east of Tokyo. It was conceived partly to bring high-level oval racing to Japan and to serve as a Honda test and heritage facility, complete with a collection hall of the company's competition machines. In 2022 it was renamed Mobility Resort Motegi.

## The circuit
The road course runs 4.801 km through 14 turns and is known for a distinctive stop-and-go character: a succession of hard braking zones into slow corners followed by short bursts of acceleration, placing heavy demands on brakes and traction rather than sustained cornering speed. It is comparatively flat by the standards of Japanese circuits. The separate oval, built to American superspeedway proportions at about 1.5 miles, occupied its own loop and could not operate at the same time as the road course.

## Racing at Motegi
The oval's signature event was the IndyCar Indy Japan 300, a rare Asian round for American open-wheel racing held from 1998 to 2011. It ran on the oval through 2010; the 2011 finale, the last IndyCar race in Japan, was switched to the road course after the Tōhoku earthquake damaged the banking, which was never raced on again and has since been decommissioned. On the road course, Motegi has hosted grand prix motorcycle racing since 1999, as the Pacific Grand Prix from 2000 to 2003 and otherwise as the Japanese Grand Prix, and it returns for the 2026 MotoGP season. The circuit has also staged Super GT, Super Formula and domestic touring car racing.

tracks.name: Okayama International Circuit
tracks.summary: Technical circuit formerly known as TI Circuit Aida that hosted the Formula One Pacific Grand Prix in 1994 and 1995.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit was the creation of golf-course magnate Hajime Tanaka, who applied the membership model of an exclusive country club to motor racing: wealthy individuals and corporations bought memberships that funded construction of a private track where they could drive their own cars. Carved from mountainous terrain near the town of Aida in Okayama Prefecture, it opened on 18 November 1990 as TI Circuit Aida, the "TI" standing for Tanaka International. Several corners were named after British racing drivers, among them Moss, Redman, Hobbs, Piper and Attwood. After Tanaka's original business folded, the venue passed to new owners and was renamed Okayama International Circuit on 1 January 2005.

## The circuit
At 3.703 km with 13 turns, the layout is compact, slow and technical, its succession of tight corners rewarding precision over outright power. The remote countryside setting, reached along narrow rural roads far from any large city, gave it a distinctive character but also created severe logistical difficulties during its brief spell on the world stage.

## Racing at Okayama
The track's international peak came in 1994 and 1995, when it hosted the Formula One Pacific Grand Prix, Japan's second world championship round in those years, staged separately from the Japanese Grand Prix held at Suzuka. Michael Schumacher won both races; his 1995 victory secured his second drivers' title. The Pacific Grand Prix was not held beyond 1995, its isolation and limited infrastructure proving decisive. The circuit has since concentrated on Japanese national motorsport, hosting rounds of Super GT, Super Formula Lights and the MFJ Superbike series; its motorcycle racing has remained at national-championship level rather than the MotoGP world championship.

tracks.name: Rally Japan
tracks.summary: Japan’s round of the World Rally Championship. The event first ran in 2004 on the gravel roads of Hokkaido, and was revived in 2022 as a tarmac rally based in the Aichi and Gifu regions around Toyota City.

tracks.name: Suzuka International Racing Course
tracks.summary: Honda-owned figure-eight circuit widely regarded as one of the greatest drivers' tracks; home of the Japanese Grand Prix and Suzuka 8 Hours.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Suzuka was built by Honda as a test facility and opened in 1962, its layout drawn up by the Dutch circuit designer John Hugenholtz. One of Japan's first purpose-built permanent road courses, it has remained in Honda ownership ever since and is operated today through the company's Mobilityland subsidiary. The site soon outgrew its testing brief to become the country's premier racing venue.

## The circuit
Measuring 5.807 km with 18 turns, Suzuka is defined by its figure-eight configuration: the back straight crosses over the pit straight on an overpass, making it the only FIA Grade 1 circuit with such a crossover layout. The lap threads together a demanding set of corners, from the flowing opening Esses and the Degner curves to the near-flat-out 130R, the long Spoon Curve and the Casio Triangle chicane before the start-finish line. Its fast, rhythmic and unforgiving character has earned it a lasting reputation as one of the sport's great tests of a driver.

## Racing at Suzuka
The circuit has staged the Formula One Japanese Grand Prix since 1987, interrupted when nearby Fuji Speedway held the race in 2007 and 2008 and by pandemic cancellations in 2020 and 2021. Its traditional late-season date long made it a championship decider, with titles settled there in 1988, 1989, 1990 and 1991 among others, including the contentious Senna–Prost collisions of 1989 and 1990. Suzuka remains on the calendar and hosted the 2026 Japanese Grand Prix. It is also home to the Suzuka 8 Hours, a motorcycle endurance race run since 1978 that ranks among the most prestigious in the discipline and draws entries from the major manufacturers.

tracks.name: Safari Rally
tracks.summary: Legendary rough, long-distance African rally, historically based around Nairobi and now Naivasha, testing cars against terrain and wildlife.

tracks.name: Guia Circuit
tracks.summary: Narrow, demanding street circuit around Guia Hill, home of the Macau Grand Prix and its famed Formula 3 and touring-car races.

tracks.name: Sepang International Circuit
tracks.summary: Sepang International Circuit near Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — Hermann Tilke's first major Formula 1 project (opened 1999). It hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017 and today hosts the Malaysian motorcycle Grand Prix (MotoGP).
tracks.article:
## Origins
Sepang was Malaysia's bid to place itself at the centre of Asian motorsport, built on former plantation land close to Kuala Lumpur International Airport. It opened on 7 March 1999 as the first purpose-built Formula One circuit designed by the German architect Hermann Tilke, and its striking main grandstand, shaded by a sweeping twin-canopy roof, set a template for the wave of Tilke-designed venues that followed at Shanghai, Bahrain, Istanbul and Abu Dhabi.

## The circuit
The 5.543 km lap runs to 15 turns and is defined by exceptionally wide track, long straights and fast, sweeping corners, with a tight hairpin linking its two main straights to promote overtaking. The generous width invites several racing lines and side-by-side running. Conditions add to the challenge: the equatorial heat and humidity punish cars and riders alike, and sudden tropical downpours have repeatedly reshaped races.

## Racing at Sepang
Sepang hosted the Formula One Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017. The inaugural race was won by Eddie Irvine for Ferrari, and the event became a long-standing flyaway fixture before rising hosting fees and falling attendance brought its Formula One tenure to an end after 2017. Motorcycle racing has proved more enduring: the circuit has held the Malaysian round of the Grand Prix motorcycle world championship since 1999 and remains on the MotoGP calendar, its late-season slot staging the 2026 Malaysian Grand Prix, with a new agreement confirmed to keep the race there through 2031.

tracks.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
tracks.summary: High-altitude Mexico City circuit whose stadium section around the old Peraltada draws huge crowds at the Mexican Grand Prix.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The circuit was built in the Magdalena Mixhuca sports park in eastern Mexico City and opened on 20 November 1959. It is named after the Rodríguez brothers, Mexico's pioneering Grand Prix drivers: Ricardo, killed in practice for the non-championship 1962 Mexican Grand Prix when his car's suspension failed at the fast Peraltada corner, and Pedro, a Formula One and sportscar race winner who died in a sportscar crash in Germany in 1971. The venue took its present name honouring both brothers in 1979.

## The circuit
The 4.304 km lap has 17 turns, but its defining feature is altitude: at roughly 2,240 metres above sea level it is the highest circuit in Formula One, the thin air cutting aerodynamic drag and downforce while straining engine cooling. The original layout ended with the long, banked Peraltada; after a 2015 redesign by Hermann Tilke, the lap now diverts through the Foro Sol baseball stadium, a natural amphitheatre packed with grandstands, before rejoining the old corner's final section onto the main straight.

## Racing in Mexico City
The Mexican Grand Prix was part of the Formula One World Championship from 1963 to 1970 and again from 1986 to 1992, before returning in 2015 as one of the sport's great spectacles. The stadium section, ringed by huge and close-packed crowds, gives the event a distinctive atmosphere, and the race now runs as the Mexico City Grand Prix. It remains on the Formula One calendar, scheduled among the late-season rounds in 2026.

tracks.name: Circuit de Monaco
tracks.summary: Tight, glamorous street circuit through Monte Carlo and the crown jewel of the Formula One calendar since 1950.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Monaco Grand Prix was the idea of Antony Noghès, an official of the Automobile Club de Monaco, who laid out a race on the principality's public roads. The first event was held in 1929 and won by William Grover-Williams in a Bugatti. When the Formula One World Championship began in 1950, Monaco was among its rounds; after a short absence it returned in 1955 and, save for the pandemic-cancelled 2020 edition, has been run every year since, becoming the most prestigious fixture on the calendar and one leg of motorsport's Triple Crown.

## The circuit
Threaded through the streets of Monte Carlo and La Condamine around the harbour, the 3.337 km lap packs 19 turns into a course with almost no run-off. From the climb out of Sainte-Dévote to Casino Square, down through Mirabeau to the Fairmont Hairpin, the slowest corner in Formula One taken at around 48 km/h, then on through the tunnel, the Nouvelle Chicane, Tabac, the Swimming Pool complex and La Rascasse, the layout has survived largely unchanged since 1929.

## Racing at Monaco
The narrow confines make overtaking exceptionally difficult, placing a premium on qualifying position and driver precision rather than raw car performance. A clean lap demands millimetric accuracy between the barriers, and small errors are heavily punished. Set against the backdrop of the harbour, the moored yachts and the surrounding hillside, the race combines sporting difficulty with a glamour no other round matches, and victory at Monaco remains among the most coveted achievements in the sport.

tracks.name: Circuit Zandvoort
tracks.summary: Seaside dunes circuit that returned to the Formula One calendar in 2021 with banked corners for the Dutch Grand Prix.
tracks.article:
## Origins
A circuit was laid out through the coastal sand dunes north of the seaside town of Zandvoort, partly following roads built during the Second World War, and opened in August 1948. It hosted the Formula One Dutch Grand Prix across several stretches, from 1950 to 1953, in 1955, and from 1958 to 1971 and 1973 to 1985, before rising costs and the loss of its slot pushed it off the calendar for more than three decades.

## The circuit
The 4.259 km lap has 14 turns and runs through the dunes with significant elevation change and fast, flowing corners. For the return of Formula One, two corners were rebuilt with steep banking: the Hugenholtz curve at Turn 3 and the final Arie Luyendyk corner at Turn 14. The banked last corner in particular was designed to let cars carry more speed onto the start-finish straight and improve the chances of overtaking into Turn 1.

## Racing at Zandvoort
The Dutch Grand Prix returned in 2021, its revival propelled by the popularity of home favourite Max Verstappen, who won each of the first three editions from 2021 to 2023 before vast orange crowds. McLaren then took over, with Lando Norris winning in 2024 and Oscar Piastri in 2025. The renewed run proved brief: organisers agreed only a final one-year extension, and the 2026 event, featuring the first Formula One sprint race held in the Netherlands, is confirmed as the last Dutch Grand Prix.

tracks.name: TT Circuit Assen
tracks.summary: TT Circuit Assen in the Netherlands — 'The Cathedral' of motorcycle racing, host of the Dutch TT every year since 1949 bar the COVID-cancelled 2020 round.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Motorcycle racing at Assen dates to 1925, when the first Dutch TT was run over public roads linking villages to the south of the town. The event outgrew those makeshift roads, and in 1955 it moved to a purpose-built permanent circuit that reused a portion of the original course. Decades of top-level competition earned the venue its enduring nickname, "the Cathedral," a reflection of the reverence that riders and enthusiasts hold for the site.

## The circuit
Assen has been reshaped several times across its history. The permanent layout was progressively shortened, and a fundamental redesign for 2006 removed the long northern loop to create the current Grand Prix configuration of roughly 4.5 kilometres and 18 turns. The track is known for its fast, flowing rhythm, its closely linked left-right transitions and a notably grippy surface, ending in a tight chicane before the start/finish line. Its sweeping curves reward carried momentum and precise line selection over heavy braking, a character that has long made it a favourite among riders.

## Racing at Assen
The Dutch TT has been part of the Grand Prix motorcycle world championship in every season since the series began in 1949 — the only circuit to have featured on every calendar — a run broken solely by the 2020 cancellation during the COVID-19 pandemic. Traditionally staged in late June, the race remains a fixture of the MotoGP schedule and appears on the 2026 calendar. Beyond MotoGP, Assen has hosted the Superbike World Championship since 1992 and rounds of the Sidecar World Championship, underlining its standing as one of the most historically significant venues in motorcycle racing.

tracks.name: Algarve International Circuit (Portimao)
tracks.summary: Undulating roller-coaster circuit at Portimao that hosts the Portuguese motorcycle Grand Prix and held the F1 Portuguese GP in 2020 and 2021.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Algarve International Circuit opened in October 2008 on hilly ground outside Portimão, in southern Portugal. Designed by the practice Ricardo Pina, Arquitectos, it was built at a cost of around 195 million euros as the centrepiece of a wider development that also includes a karting track, a technology park, a hotel and apartments. The facility holds an FIA Grade 1 licence, the highest classification available, allowing it to host the top tiers of car and motorcycle racing.

## The circuit
The 4.653-kilometre track is defined above all by its dramatic elevation changes. Steep climbs, sudden crests and blind, plunging corners have drawn frequent comparison to older road courses such as Spa-Francorchamps, and drivers routinely liken a lap to a roller-coaster. Its 15 turns wind across the gradients so that apexes and braking points are often hidden beyond a rise, placing a premium on commitment and circuit knowledge. The long start/finish straight feeds into a downhill right-hander that sets the tone for the lap.

## Racing at Portimão
Portimão hosted the Formula One Portuguese Grand Prix twice, in 2020 and 2021, both editions added amid the disruption of the COVID-19 pandemic and both won by Lewis Hamilton; his 2020 victory was the record-breaking 92nd of his career. The circuit is contracted to return to the Formula One calendar in 2027 and 2028. In MotoGP it has staged the Portuguese Grand Prix every year since 2020 and features on the 2026 schedule. World Superbikes and endurance championships have also raced there since the venue opened.

tracks.name: Autodromo do Estoril
tracks.summary: Circuit near Lisbon that hosted the Portuguese Grand Prix from 1984 to 1996, including Ayrton Senna's first F1 win.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Autódromo do Estoril opened on 17 June 1972, built on a plateau near Alcabideche, roughly 30 kilometres west of Lisbon and close to the resort town of Estoril that lent the circuit its name. The surrounding area had staged motor racing in earlier decades, but the permanent track gave Portugal a modern, purpose-built home for international competition.

## The circuit
The 4.182-kilometre lap runs across noticeable elevation changes and is anchored by a start/finish straight approaching one kilometre in length. The layout mixes fast sweeps with a pair of hairpins and a long, demanding final right-hander onto the pit straight that has decided several races. Its exposed, coastal setting frequently brings gusting wind that adds to the challenge for cars and motorcycles alike.

## Racing at Estoril
Estoril hosted the Formula One Portuguese Grand Prix from 1984 to 1996. The 1985 race produced Ayrton Senna's first Formula One victory, a dominant drive in torrential rain, while the 1996 event is remembered for Jacques Villeneuve's pass around the outside of Michael Schumacher at the final corner. Formula One left after 1996 amid concerns over the circuit's safety standards. The venue went on to host the Portuguese motorcycle Grand Prix from 2000 to 2012, running MotoGP and its supporting classes for thirteen consecutive years. Estoril no longer appears on the Formula One or MotoGP calendars, but it remains in active use, hosting the Superbike World Championship and a range of other international and national events.

tracks.name: Rally de Portugal
tracks.summary: Fast, sandy gravel rally now based in the north around Matosinhos, one of the best-attended events on the WRC calendar.

tracks.name: Lusail International Circuit
tracks.summary: Floodlit circuit near Doha built for MotoGP in 2004 that added the Qatar Grand Prix to the Formula One calendar in 2021.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Lusail International Circuit was built near Doha, Qatar, and opened on 30 September 2004, constructed in under a year specifically to bring Grand Prix motorcycle racing to the Middle East. In 2007 the venue installed an extensive permanent floodlighting system, at the time the largest sports-lighting project of its kind in the world, turning it into a night-racing facility.

## The circuit
The circuit measures around 5.4 kilometres with 16 turns and is dominated by a main straight of more than one kilometre that produces high top speeds and heavy braking. A mix of medium and high-speed corners follows, run on a surface surrounded by desert sand that is a persistent complication for grip. Ahead of Formula One's regular arrival the facility was extensively renovated for 2023, its grandstands rebuilt to raise capacity from 8,000 to 52,000.

## Racing at Lusail
Lusail has hosted a round of the MotoGP world championship since 2004, and in 2008 it staged the first night race in the championship's history. For much of its history the Qatar round opened the MotoGP season under floodlights; for 2026 it was moved to November. Formula One first visited in 2021, when Lewis Hamilton won a one-off Qatar Grand Prix during his title fight with Max Verstappen; after no race in 2022 it became a permanent fixture from 2023, with Verstappen winning in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Both championships feature on the 2026 calendar, the Formula One race scheduled for late November.

tracks.name: Jeddah Corniche Circuit
tracks.summary: An exceptionally fast street circuit along the Red Sea corniche in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia — billed as the fastest street circuit in Formula 1 and one of the longest, with 27 corners.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Jeddah Corniche Circuit was laid out along the Red Sea waterfront in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and opened on 3 December 2021. Designed by Carsten Tilke, it was completed on a rapid timeline after ground was broken only in March of the same year, giving Saudi Arabia its first Formula One venue as a street course threaded through the coastal Corniche district.

## The circuit
At 6.174 kilometres the circuit is the third longest on the Formula One calendar, behind only Spa-Francorchamps and the Las Vegas Strip Circuit. Its 27 corners are mostly fast, flowing sweeps lined by unforgiving walls, a combination that produces the highest average speeds of any street circuit in Formula One; pole position in 2025 was set at over 250 km/h. Three DRS zones and a series of blind, high-commitment kinks make it one of the most demanding and hazardous layouts on the schedule.

## Racing at Jeddah
The inaugural Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, held on 5 December 2021, was won by Lewis Hamilton after a chaotic, incident-strewn duel with Max Verstappen that drew the pair level on points before the season finale. The race became an annual fixture, run in March through 2024 and in April from 2025, and the circuit has also welcomed Formula E, Formula 2 and other categories. The 2026 Saudi Arabian Grand Prix, however, was cancelled along with the Bahrain round after the outbreak of regional conflict early in the year, leaving Jeddah off the 2026 Formula One schedule.

tracks.name: Marina Bay Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Downtown street circuit that hosted Formula One's first night race in 2008; reconfigured to 19 turns from 2023.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Marina Bay Street Circuit was created for the 2008 Singapore Grand Prix, which on 28 September 2008 became the first night race in Formula One history, run under floodlights through the downtown streets beside Marina Bay. The inaugural event was later mired in controversy when it emerged that Renault had ordered Nelson Piquet Jr to crash deliberately to engineer a win for his team-mate Fernando Alonso, the affair that became known as "Crashgate."

## The circuit
The lap runs for close to five kilometres through the city, hemmed in by concrete walls and lined with landmarks. For 2023 the circuit was reconfigured, a slow, wall-lined section replaced by a new straight that cut the turn count from 23 to 19 and trimmed lap times substantially. Notoriously bumpy and run in high heat and humidity, it ranks among the most physically punishing events of the season, and the mix of walls and long race duration long made safety-car interventions almost routine.

## Racing at Marina Bay
The Singapore Grand Prix has been held every year since 2008, the only exceptions being 2020 and 2021, when the race was cancelled during the COVID-19 pandemic. The night-time event became one of the sport's most recognisable races, known for its city-skyline backdrop and its reputation for attrition and unpredictable results. The circuit remains firmly on the Formula One calendar and is scheduled to host a round of the 2026 season in October.

tracks.name: Kyalami Circuit
tracks.summary: High-veld circuit near Johannesburg that hosted the South African Grand Prix and remains the country's premier racing venue.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Kyalami opened on 4 November 1961 on the high-veld plateau at Midrand, between Johannesburg and Pretoria in what is now Gauteng. The name comes from a Zulu phrase meaning "my home." Its altitude of roughly 1,500 metres thins the air, cutting engine power and aerodynamic grip — a defining trait that has shaped car set-up and race strategy for more than six decades. The circuit quickly became the focus of South African motor racing and, from 1967, the home of the country's world-championship Grand Prix.

## The circuit
The original layout was a fast, flowing track famed for its long main straight and the daunting Crowthorne corner at its end. In 1987 the land was sold for commercial development, and the circuit was rebuilt in 1989 on a smaller, tighter site that sacrificed much of its open character. A comprehensive 2015 upgrade modernised the facilities and secured FIA Grade 2 status. The current Grand Prix configuration measures about 4.52 km with 16 turns and retains significant elevation change across the veld.

## Racing at Kyalami
Kyalami staged the South African Grand Prix regularly from 1967 to 1985 before political and commercial pressures ended that run; Formula 1 briefly returned in 1992 and 1993 on the rebuilt layout. The venue has since anchored South African national racing and, from 2019, the revived Kyalami 9 Hours endurance event. Formula 1 has not returned since 1993, though the owners have won approval for a Grade 1 upgrade and the South African government has backed a bid to bring the Grand Prix back from 2027; as of 2026 no date is confirmed.

tracks.name: Korea International Circuit
tracks.summary: Coastal circuit near Yeongam that held the Korean Grand Prix from 2010 to 2013.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Korea International Circuit was built near Yeongam in South Jeolla Province, about 320 km south of Seoul and close to the port of Mokpo. Designed by Hermann Tilke, it opened in 2010 under a deal between commercial-rights holder Bernie Ecclestone and the Korea Auto Valley Operation, as the centrepiece of an ambitious plan for a motorsport hub and an adjoining marina city. Construction ran late, and the track was finished only weeks before its first race.

## The circuit
Tilke's design paired a permanent racing section with a semi-street layout meant to thread through the planned coastal development. The 5.615 km lap features 18 turns and, when new, one of the longest straights in Formula 1, feeding a heavy-braking right-hander built for overtaking. The blend of long straights and slow, technical corners was demanding on brakes and traction, but the surrounding city that was supposed to grow up around the circuit never materialised.

## Racing at Yeongam
The circuit hosted the Korean Grand Prix for four seasons, from 2010 to 2013. The inaugural race in 2010 was run in treacherous wet conditions and won by Fernando Alonso. Despite that early promise, poor attendance, the remote location and heavy financial losses undermined the event, and Korea fell off the Formula 1 calendar after 2013 without being formally replaced. The venue has since hosted South Korea's Superrace Championship and occasional international touring-car events, but has never regained a place in world-championship motor racing.

tracks.name: Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya
tracks.summary: A modern circuit near Barcelona and long the home of the Spanish Grand Prix — renamed the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix for 2026, with the Spanish GP title moving to Madrid. For years it was also Formula 1's main pre-season testing venue, before testing moved to Bahrain.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya opened in September 1991 at Montmeló, around 20 km north of Barcelona, built to give Catalonia a permanent home for international motor racing. It hosted the Spanish Grand Prix in its debut season and has been a fixture of both Formula 1 and Grand Prix motorcycle racing ever since, becoming one of the most familiar circuits to drivers, riders and engineers alike.

## The circuit
The 4.657 km lap combines long, fast corners with a tight, technical final sector, and its abrasive surface and full range of corner types made it a definitive proving ground for chassis and tyres. For many years it was Formula 1's principal pre-season testing venue, so thoroughly understood that teams could benchmark set-ups against seasons of accumulated data — a role that has since passed to Bahrain. A chicane has been added and removed near the end of the lap over the years, and MotoGP and F1 have at times run slightly different layouts.

## Racing at Catalunya
The circuit was long the home of the Spanish Grand Prix, staging it every year from 1991. For 2026 that changed: the Spanish Grand Prix title moved to a new street circuit around Madrid's IFEMA exhibition centre, and the Barcelona race was renamed the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, scheduled to alternate with the Belgian Grand Prix in the seasons that follow. The venue also hosts the Catalan motorcycle Grand Prix, a mainstay of the MotoGP calendar, and remains one of Spain's busiest and most historically important racing facilities.

tracks.name: Circuit Ricardo Tormo
tracks.summary: Stadium-style circuit at Cheste near Valencia that traditionally closes the MotoGP season with the Valencian Community Grand Prix.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Circuit Ricardo Tormo opened in 1999 at Cheste, about 20 km west of the city of Valencia. It was named in honour of Ricardo Tormo, the Valencian rider who won two 50cc world championships and died of leukaemia in 1998, shortly before the track bearing his name was completed. From the start it was conceived as a compact, spectator-focused arena rather than a sprawling road course.

## The circuit
The 4.005 km lap runs anti-clockwise through 14 turns inside a natural bowl, with grandstands wrapped around the infield so that spectators can see almost the entire circuit from one seat — a stadium-style design unusual among Grand Prix venues. Its mix of tight, low-gear corners and a long main straight rewards braking and agility over outright top speed, while its late-November date often brings cool, unpredictable weather. The circuit also serves as a year-round testing base for MotoGP.

## Racing at Valencia
The circuit has hosted the Valencian Community Grand Prix almost every year since 1999, traditionally as the final round of the MotoGP season and the stage on which numerous titles have been settled. That tradition was broken in 2024, when catastrophic flooding across the Valencia region in late October forced the finale to be cancelled and a replacement round staged at Barcelona. Valencia returned to its closing slot in 2025 and is the scheduled 2026 season finale, its future secured by a contract that runs to 2031.

tracks.name: Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto
tracks.summary: Andalusian circuit that hosts the Spanish motorcycle Grand Prix and staged the Spanish and European F1 Grands Prix in the late 1980s and 1990s.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Circuito de Jerez opened in 1985 outside Jerez de la Frontera, in the sherry-producing heart of Andalusia in southern Spain. It was renamed the Circuito de Jerez - Ángel Nieto in 2018 in memory of the thirteen-time motorcycling world champion, who had died the previous year. The circuit rapidly became the centre of Spanish motorcycle racing and a passionate focal point for the sport's vast local following.

## The circuit
The lap of roughly 4.4 km is a tight, technical sequence of medium- and low-speed corners with little respite, placing a premium on mechanical grip, braking and rhythm rather than top speed. Its best-known corner is the tight right-hander at the end of the lap, now named after Jorge Lorenzo, a classic overtaking and last-lap ambush point. Warm Andalusian weather and an amphitheatre-like setting draw huge crowds, especially for the motorcycle Grand Prix each spring.

## Racing at Jerez
Jerez staged the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix from 1986 to 1990 and then the European Grand Prix in 1994 and 1997. The 1997 race decided the world championship and is remembered for Michael Schumacher's failed attempt to force Jacques Villeneuve off the road; a subsequent controversy, when the local mayor gatecrashed the podium ceremony, soured relations with Formula 1 and the championship did not return. Jerez has hosted the Spanish motorcycle Grand Prix almost every year since 1987 and remains a permanent fixture of the MotoGP calendar, confirmed again for 2026, as well as a major World Superbike and testing venue.

tracks.name: Circuito del Jarama
tracks.summary: Tight, twisting circuit north of Madrid that hosted nine Spanish Grands Prix between 1968 and 1981.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Circuito del Jarama opened in 1967 on arid scrubland at San Sebastián de los Reyes, about 30 km north of Madrid. It was designed by the Dutchman John Hugenholtz, the man behind Suzuka, who packed a demanding sequence of corners into a compact site. The circuit gave central Spain a permanent racing venue and soon took its turn hosting the country's Formula 1 Grand Prix.

## The circuit
Just under 4 km long, Jarama is a tight, twisting track with a short main straight and a rapid-fire run of corners that leaves little room to overtake. That narrowness produced processional but tense racing and ultimately drove Formula 1 away, as cars grew wider and faster than the layout could comfortably hold. The circuit has been modified and lengthened since its Grand Prix days and remains in regular use for national and international motorsport.

## Racing at Jarama
Jarama hosted the Spanish Grand Prix nine times between 1968 and 1981, for much of that period alternating with Montjuïc in Barcelona. Its final Formula 1 race, in 1981, is among the sport's most celebrated: Gilles Villeneuve held off a train of four faster cars in his unwieldy turbo Ferrari, the top five covered by just over a second at the flag. After 1981 the Grand Prix moved on and Jarama settled into a long life of touring cars, sports cars and motorcycle racing. In March 2026 it hosted the inaugural Madrid E-Prix, becoming the longest circuit yet raced on by Formula E.

tracks.name: Circuito Internacional de Zuera
tracks.summary: International kart circuit north of Zaragoza in Aragon, an FIA Karting venue also used by motorcycles.

tracks.name: Montjuic Circuit
tracks.summary: Park street circuit in Barcelona whose fast, dangerous layout hosted the Spanish Grand Prix until a fatal 1975 accident ended F1 racing there.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Racing on Montjuïc, the wooded hill overlooking Barcelona's harbour, began in 1932, and a permanent street layout through the park was fixed in 1933. The Penya Rhin Grand Prix ran there through the 1930s, drawing pre-war stars such as Tazio Nuvolari, before competition was interrupted by the Spanish Civil War and the Second World War. Racing resumed afterwards, and from the 1950s the parkland course built a reputation as one of Europe's most spectacular and most feared.

## The circuit
The 3.791 km lap ran anticlockwise through the park's public roads, climbing and dropping across the hillside over twelve turns. Its character was split: one half was slow and tight, the other flowed fast between trees, kerbs and unforgiving barriers, so that setting a car up well meant compromising. Many competitors regarded the layout as inherently unsafe, and unease about the Armco barriers lining it grew through the early 1970s.

## Racing at Montjuïc
Montjuïc held the Spanish Grand Prix four times — in 1969, 1971, 1973 and 1975 — alternating with Madrid's Jarama. The 1975 race became its last. Drivers protested that the barriers were improperly bolted and at first refused to practise. On lap 26 the rear wing of Rolf Stommelen's Embassy Hill car failed; the machine cleared the barrier and killed four people, among them a fireman, a spectator and two photographers. The race was stopped on lap 29 with Jochen Mass leading, and half points were awarded for the first time in World Championship history — the ruling that left Lella Lombardi with the half-point that remains the only score by a woman in Formula One. Grand Prix racing never returned; motorcycle Grands Prix continued until 1976 and sports car events into the 1980s.

tracks.name: MotorLand Aragon
tracks.summary: Tilke-designed circuit near Alcaniz in Aragon that hosts the Aragon motorcycle Grand Prix and World Superbike rounds.
tracks.article:
## Origins
MotorLand Aragón was built on the arid uplands near Alcañiz, in Spain's Aragón region. The permanent circuit was designed by Hermann Tilke in collaboration with the architecture practice Foster + Partners, with the former Formula One driver Pedro de la Rosa acting as a technical and sporting consultant. Ground was broken in December 2005, and the complex opened on 6 September 2009 as the centrepiece of a wider development combining motorsport, technology and leisure facilities.

## The circuit
The Grand Prix layout used by motorcycles measures 5.077 km and links 17 corners. It combines fast straights and a downhill run with a technical, stop-start middle sector and a long final left-hander onto the main straight, and the site carries noticeable elevation change, placing a premium on braking and tyre management. Alternative configurations, including a longer 5.345 km layout for cars and a shorter national circuit, share the same infrastructure.

## Racing at Aragón
The circuit joined the MotoGP World Championship in 2010, and the Aragon Grand Prix remains on the 2026 calendar. The Superbike World Championship has visited since 2011 and is contracted through 2027, making Aragón one of the series' regular Spanish rounds. The venue has also hosted car championships over the years, among them the World Series by Renault and Formula V8 3.5 until 2017, the World Touring Car Cup between 2020 and 2022, and a European Le Mans Series round in 2023. It remains one of Spain's busiest international racing facilities.

tracks.name: Pedralbes Circuit
tracks.summary: Fast street circuit on the wide avenues of Barcelona that held the Spanish Grand Prix in 1951 and 1954.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Pedralbes Circuit was laid out in 1946 on the broad avenues of the Pedralbes district, in the western outskirts of Barcelona. Its wide, fast public roads appealed at once to drivers and spectators, and the venue staged several runnings of the Penya Rhin Grand Prix in the late 1940s and early 1950s before it was chosen to hold Spain's round of the new Formula One World Championship.

## The circuit
The lap measured 6.316 km and was built for speed. Long straights along the city's avenues were joined by broad, sweeping corners rather than tight turns, letting the front-running cars of the era average high speeds. The course was widely admired, but as those speeds rose it offered little protection to the crowds at the roadside — a weakness that would count against it.

## Racing at Pedralbes
Pedralbes held the Spanish Grand Prix twice as a World Championship event. In 1951 the race decided the title: Juan Manuel Fangio won in his Alfa Romeo 159 to secure the first of his five championships, ahead of the Ferraris. The Grand Prix returned in 1954 for the debut of Lancia's new D50. Alberto Ascari put the Lancia on pole and set the fastest lap but retired with clutch trouble, and Mike Hawthorn won for Ferrari, ahead of Luigi Musso and Fangio. It was the circuit's final Grand Prix. After the 1955 Le Mans disaster, tightened safety expectations made the fast, exposed street course untenable, and championship racing never came back.

tracks.name: Valencia Street Circuit
tracks.summary: Harbourside street circuit that hosted the European Grand Prix from 2008 to 2012, crossing a swing bridge over the marina.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Valencia Street Circuit was created to bring Formula One to Spain's Mediterranean coast, using the roads around the harbour that the city had redeveloped for the 2007 America's Cup. The promoter Valmor Sport, fronted by the former motorcycle racer Jorge Martínez, known as Aspar, signed a seven-year deal with Bernie Ecclestone in 2007, and Hermann Tilke laid out a course through the port. It opened in 2008.

## The circuit
At 5.419 km, the lap ran past the marina and dockside buildings through 25 corners — 11 left and 14 right. Its signature feature was a 140-metre swing bridge that carried the cars across the harbour channel. Long straights allowed speeds of around 320 km/h, but the succession of ninety-degree turns between concrete walls made overtaking hard, and the layout was criticised for producing processional races.

## Racing at Valencia
The circuit staged the European Grand Prix five times, from 2008 to 2012. Felipe Massa won the inaugural race for Ferrari in 2008. The 2010 event featured a violent accident in which Mark Webber's Red Bull was launched into the air after clipping the back of Heikki Kovalainen's car; Webber walked away unhurt. The most celebrated race came in 2012, when Fernando Alonso won his home Grand Prix from eleventh on the grid. It was the last Formula One race held there: a plan to alternate the Spanish Grand Prix between Valencia and Barcelona collapsed, and the circuit was left abandoned. As of 2026 the street circuit remains disused, with no motor racing held there since.

tracks.name: Rally Sweden
tracks.summary: The only true winter round of the World Rally Championship, run on snow and ice with studded tyres; now based around Umea in the north.

tracks.name: Scandinavian Raceway (Anderstorp)
tracks.summary: Circuit at Anderstorp, built partly around an airfield, that hosted the Swedish Grand Prix from 1973 to 1978. It remains an active circuit for Swedish national racing and track days.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Scandinavian Raceway was built at Anderstorp, in the forests of southern Sweden, and opened in 1968. It was laid out on low-lying marshland, and its most distinctive feature came from an adjoining airfield: the long main straight doubles as an aircraft runway, still used by light aircraft. The permanent track gave Swedish motorsport a venue able to host international championships.

## The circuit
The lap measured just over 4 km and was unusually flat, spread across the reclaimed marsh. It combined the very long airfield straight with a series of medium- and low-speed corners, several of them banked. One quirk set it apart from almost every other Grand Prix venue: the pit lane lay roughly halfway around the lap rather than along the main straight, a consequence of the airfield layout.

## Racing at Anderstorp
Anderstorp held the Swedish Grand Prix six times, from 1973 to 1978. Denny Hulme won the first for McLaren; the local favourite Ronnie Peterson took pole but finished second, the closest any Swede came to winning at home. The 1976 race produced the only Grand Prix win for a six-wheeled car, Jody Scheckter leading a Tyrrell P34 one-two ahead of Patrick Depailler. Two years later Niki Lauda won in Brabham's radical BT46B, the so-called fan car, on its only race appearance, after which it was withdrawn. Formula One left following 1978, its Swedish audience thinned by the deaths of Peterson and Gunnar Nilsson that year. The circuit remains active, hosting national and Nordic championships including the Porsche Carrera Cup Scandinavia.

tracks.name: Circuit Bremgarten
tracks.summary: Tree-lined forest circuit near Bern that hosted the Swiss Grand Prix until circuit racing was banned in Switzerland after the 1955 Le Mans disaster.
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Bremgarten circuit was established in 1931 as a motorcycle course in the Bremgartenwald, the forest on the northwestern edge of Bern. It ran on public roads through the woods, hosting motorcycle racing from the outset and, from 1934, the Swiss Grand Prix for cars, and it quickly became a fixture of pre-war European racing.

## The circuit
At 7.28 km the lap was a near-continuous chain of fast, curving roads with no true straight. Because it ran beneath the forest canopy, drivers passed constantly between bright sunlight and deep shadow while the road surface changed grip from one stretch to the next; in the wet it turned treacherous. Those hazards, with trees and banks close to the edge, made Bremgarten one of the most dangerous circuits of its era. It claimed several lives, among them the motorcyclist Omobono Tenni and the driver Achille Varzi, both killed in 1948.

## Racing at Bremgarten
Before the war the Grand Prix drew the dominant German teams, Rudolf Caracciola winning three times for Mercedes. After 1945 the Swiss Grand Prix became part of the Formula One World Championship from its inaugural 1950 season: Giuseppe Farina won that first year for Alfa Romeo, Piero Taruffi took 1952 for Ferrari, Alberto Ascari won in 1953, and Juan Manuel Fangio triumphed in both 1951 and 1954. Fangio's 1954 victory in a Mercedes W196 proved to be the last race held at the circuit. After the 1955 Le Mans disaster, Switzerland banned circuit racing outright and the scheduled Swiss Grand Prix was cancelled. No motor race has been held at Bremgarten since, and the national ban endured for more than seventy years, until it was finally lifted in 2026.

tracks.name: Buriram International Circuit (Chang)
tracks.summary: Tilke-designed circuit in Buriram, Thailand's first FIA Grade 1 track and host of the Thailand motorcycle Grand Prix.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Buriram International Circuit was built by Newin Chidchob, a local politician and owner of the football club Buriram United, as the centrepiece of a sports complex in Thailand's north-east. Designed by Hermann Tilke and constructed in a reported 422 days, it opened in October 2014 as the first circuit in Thailand to hold FIA Grade 1 homologation — the standard required for Formula One. A round of Japan's Super GT series inaugurated the track over the weekend of 4-5 October 2014. It trades commercially as the Chang International Circuit, after its brewery title sponsor.

## The circuit
The lap runs 4.554 km over 12 turns, combining long straights with hard braking zones and flowing direction changes that place a premium on stability under braking. Two artificial lakes sit inside the perimeter, added to aid air circulation in the region's heat and humidity, and the circuit was floodlit to FIA standards from the outset with night running in mind. Its flat terrain and generous run-off make it forgiving by modern standards, while the succession of heavy stops rewards strong traction and cooling.

## Racing at Buriram
World Superbike arrived first, in 2015, with Jonathan Rea winning both races of the inaugural meeting. MotoGP followed in 2018, Marc Marquez taking the first premier-class Thailand Grand Prix. The event became a fixture and in recent seasons has opened the championship: 2026 marked the second running of the Thai round as the season-opener. Dorna has confirmed the Grand Prix on the calendar through 2031. The venue has also hosted the Asian Le Mans Series and the World Touring Car Championship, though a Formula One race has never materialised.

tracks.name: Istanbul Park
tracks.summary: A modern circuit on the Asian side of Istanbul, Turkey, famous for the multi-apex Turn 8. It hosted the Turkish Grand Prix from 2005 to 2011 and again in 2020-2021; a 2026 agreement returns Formula 1 for 2027-2031.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Istanbul Park opened in 2005 in the Tuzla district on the Asian side of the Bosphorus, part of a wave of Hermann Tilke-designed venues added to the Formula One calendar in the 2000s. It staged the inaugural Turkish Grand Prix that August. The circuit was praised on arrival for its natural elevation changes and flowing layout, and came to be regarded as one of the more accomplished of the era's purpose-built tracks.

## The circuit
The 5.338 km lap is one of a small number on the calendar run anti-clockwise, and its defining feature is Turn 8 — a long, high-speed left-hander taken through four apexes that loads the neck and tyres over several seconds. Combined with steep gradients and a fast run down to the final corners, the layout rewards commitment and punishes understeer, and it has consistently drawn praise from drivers.

## Racing at Istanbul Park
The circuit hosted the Turkish Grand Prix from 2005 to 2011, a spell defined by Felipe Massa, who won three times for Ferrari between 2006 and 2008. Financial pressures dropped it from the schedule after 2011, but it returned in 2020 and 2021: Lewis Hamilton clinched his seventh world title there in 2020, and Valtteri Bottas won the last race of the second spell in 2021. MotoGP visited from 2005 to 2007, and the venue also held World Touring Car and rallycross rounds. In April 2026 Formula One announced a five-year agreement to return the Turkish Grand Prix to Istanbul Park from 2027 through 2031.

tracks.name: Yas Marina Circuit
tracks.summary: Abu Dhabi circuit on Yas Island, traditional season finale of the Formula One calendar and a day-to-night race.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Yas Marina Circuit opened in 2009 on Yas Island, a purpose-built leisure and entertainment development in Abu Dhabi. Designed by Hermann Tilke, it hosted the first Abu Dhabi Grand Prix in November 2009 and introduced Formula One's first day-to-night race, the running beginning in daylight and finishing under floodlights against the harbour and the hotel that straddles the track.

## The circuit
As first built the lap ran 5.554 km over 21 corners but drew criticism for poor overtaking. For 2021 it was reprofiled to 5.281 km and 16 turns, with a tightened hairpin and a long banked corner opening up the flow toward the marina, changes that improved wheel-to-wheel racing. The permanently lit facility passes beneath the W Abu Dhabi hotel, and its smooth, low-abrasion surface tends to be gentle on tyres.

## Racing at Yas Marina
The Abu Dhabi Grand Prix has closed the season in most years since the circuit's 2009 debut, an unbroken run as the finale since 2014, and does so again in 2026 with the race set for 6 December. Several titles have been settled there, most controversially in 2021, when a late safety-car restart handed Max Verstappen the championship over Lewis Hamilton on the final lap. The circuit also stages Formula 2 support races and endurance events, and the post-season test has become a calendar fixture.

tracks.name: Aintree Motor Racing Circuit
tracks.summary: Circuit around the Aintree horse-racing course near Liverpool that hosted the British Grand Prix five times, including Stirling Moss's 1955 home win.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Aintree Motor Racing Circuit was built in the winter of 1953-54 around the perimeter of the famous horse-racing course near Liverpool, home of the Grand National. Mirabel Topham, whose family had bought the racecourse from Lord Sefton in 1949, conceived it after a visit to Goodwood, hoping a motor circuit sharing the existing grandstands would help the estate pay its way. The track opened in May 1954 and was soon dubbed the "Goodwood of the North".

## The circuit
The full Grand Prix circuit measured 4.828 km (3 miles) and ran on flat, exposed ground inside and alongside the horse-racing track. It was fast but relatively featureless, its challenge lying in sustained speed and its ready-made spectator facilities rather than gradient or dramatic corners. A shorter 2.470 km club circuit shares much of the same infrastructure and remains in use for sprints, track days and club-level car and motorcycle events; the full Grand Prix layout was last raced in 1964, when Jack Brabham won a non-championship Formula One race.

## Racing at Aintree
Aintree hosted the British Grand Prix five times — in 1955, 1957, 1959, 1961 and 1962 — alternating the race with Silverstone. The 1955 event became one of the most celebrated in British motor racing when Stirling Moss won his home Grand Prix for the first time, driving a Mercedes ahead of team-mate Juan Manuel Fangio to become the first British winner of the race. Two years later Moss and Tony Brooks shared the winning Vanwall, the first British Grand Prix victory for a British car. Top-level racing ended in the mid-1960s as safety demands and purpose-built rivals moved the sport on, but the club circuit has kept the site active ever since.

tracks.name: Brands Hatch
tracks.summary: Kent circuit set in a natural amphitheatre that alternated the British Grand Prix with Silverstone into the 1980s and remains a busy national venue.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Brands Hatch began as a grass-track venue in a natural chalk hollow in Kent, used by cyclists and then motorcyclists from the 1920s. A surfaced circuit opened in April 1950, and through the following decade the track was extended and upgraded, growing from a short kidney-shaped loop into a full Grand Prix circuit that climbs and falls across the sides of its natural amphitheatre.

## The circuit
The Grand Prix circuit measures 3.916 km; the shorter Indy layout, at 1.944 km, keeps to the natural bowl, where spectators can see almost the entire lap. The signature corner is Paddock Hill Bend, a fast right-hander that drops away steeply just after the start line, leading to the climb up to the Druids hairpin. Blind crests, cambered corners and near-constant elevation change have long made the circuit both a favourite of drivers and an unforgiving one.

## Racing at Brands Hatch
Brands Hatch hosted the British Grand Prix twelve times between 1964 and 1986, alternating with Silverstone, and staged the European Grand Prix in 1983 and 1985. The final Formula One race there was the 1986 British Grand Prix, won by Nigel Mansell. Endurance racing was long a fixture too: the circuit held rounds of the World Sportscar Championship, among them the 1000 km of Brands Hatch, remembered for Pedro Rodríguez's drive in the wet in 1970. Formula One did not return after 1986 as safety and capacity requirements outgrew the site, but the circuit remains one of Britain's busiest, anchoring the British Touring Car Championship, British Superbikes and a full national calendar.

tracks.name: PF International Kart Circuit
tracks.summary: The UK's premier kart circuit at Brandon near Grantham, and the only British short-circuit track holding a CIK-FIA International A licence.

tracks.name: Rally GB (Wales)
tracks.summary: Britain’s round of the World Rally Championship until 2019, run on the forest gravel of Wales. Descended from the historic RAC Rally, one of the sport’s oldest events.

tracks.name: Rockingham Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: Corby oval-and-road complex, one of Europe's few banked speedways, that briefly hosted American CART races before closing to racing in 2018.

tracks.name: Rowrah Kart Circuit
tracks.summary: Cumbrian kart circuit laid out in a disused quarry, an early proving ground for British F1 drivers including Lewis Hamilton and George Russell.

tracks.name: Silverstone Circuit
tracks.summary: Former WWII airfield that hosted the first FIA Formula One World Championship race in 1950; permanent home of the British Grand Prix and British MotoGP.
tracks.article:
## Origins

Silverstone was built not as a racetrack but as a wartime airfield. RAF Silverstone operated as a bomber station from 1943, and when the war ended its wide runways and perimeter roads were repurposed for motor racing. The first British Grand Prix was held there in 1948, and in 1950 Silverstone staged the inaugural round of the new FIA Formula One World Championship — the first world-championship Grand Prix ever run, won by Giuseppe Farina for Alfa Romeo.

## The circuit

The modern Grand Prix layout measures 5.891 km across 18 turns and is defined by its high average speed. Its most celebrated section is the Maggotts–Becketts–Chapel sequence, a rapid series of direction changes regarded as one of the great tests of a Formula One car's high-speed balance. The long Hangar Straight, the fast entry at Copse and the heavy braking zone at Stowe complete a circuit that rewards aerodynamic stability and driver commitment.

## Racing at Silverstone

Although the British Grand Prix rotated between Silverstone, Aintree and Brands Hatch for much of the mid-20th century, it has been held at Silverstone continuously since 1987 and remains one of the best-attended races of the season. The venue also hosts the British round of MotoGP, rounds of the British Touring Car and British GT championships, and endurance racing in the European Le Mans Series. The Formula One lap record stands at 1:27.097, set by Max Verstappen for Red Bull in 2020.

tracks.name: Atlanta Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: 1.54-mile Georgia quad-oval reprofiled in 2022 with steeper banking to produce superspeedway-style pack racing.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Atlanta Motor Speedway opened in 1960 as Atlanta International Raceway, a 1.5-mile oval in Hampton, Georgia, south of the city. Financial trouble dogged its early years — the track entered bankruptcy in 1971 — until Bruton Smith's Speedway Motorsports bought it in 1990 and began a long modernisation. It was renamed Atlanta Motor Speedway that year, and in 2025 took on the title EchoPark Speedway under a naming-rights deal.

## The circuit
In 1997 the layout was rebuilt into a quad-oval: the start/finish line moved to a new dogleg and the old front straight became the back straight. The defining change came ahead of the 2022 season, when the 1.54-mile (2.478 km) surface was repaved for the first time since 1997 and the corner banking raised from 24 to 28 degrees, the racing surface narrowed from 55 to 40 feet. The steeper, tighter configuration turned Atlanta into a drafting track, producing the tightly bunched pack racing previously associated with the far larger Daytona and Talladega superspeedways.

## Racing at Atlanta
Atlanta has held NASCAR Cup Series racing since the track opened in 1960 and now stages two Cup weekends a year. Its abrasive old surface had made it a tyre-management circuit prized by veteran drivers; the reprofiled track instead delivers three-wide pack racing and frequent lead changes, a divisive shift that split driver opinion when it arrived. In 2026 the venue holds two Cup Series rounds, in February and July, the latter a night race, alongside supporting NASCAR series.

tracks.name: Auto Club Speedway
tracks.summary: A fast, abrasive two-mile D-shaped oval in Fontana, California, long a NASCAR favourite for its worn, multi-groove racing. It held its final NASCAR Cup race in 2023 and has since been largely demolished for redevelopment.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Auto Club Speedway was built on the site of the abandoned Kaiser Steel mill in Fontana, California, a project announced by Roger Penske and Kaiser Steel in 1994. Constructed by Penske Motorsports and requiring extensive environmental clean-up of the old plant, the two-mile oval opened on 20 June 1997 as California Speedway. It was later owned by International Speedway Corporation and renamed Auto Club Speedway in February 2008 under a naming-rights agreement with the Automobile Club of Southern California.

## The circuit
The D-shaped oval measured 2.0 miles (3.219 km), with four turns banked at 14 degrees and a long, sweeping frontstretch. Its asphalt was left to age rather than being resurfaced for many years, and the resulting abrasive, low-grip surface wore tyres heavily while opening up several racing lines. That combination of high speed and worn pavement made it one of the more demanding intermediate ovals in American racing and encouraged wide, side-by-side competition.

## Racing at Fontana
The speedway hosted NASCAR Cup Series racing from 1997 until 2023, when Kyle Busch won the final Cup event there on 26 February 2023. CART and Champ Car open-wheel races were held from 1997 to 2002, and the IndyCar Series competed from 2002 to 2005 and again from 2012 to 2015. Plans filed in 2020 proposed replacing the superspeedway with a half-mile, high-banked short track, and demolition began in October 2023. The reconstruction was subsequently put on hold amid rising costs, and much of the land was sold for warehouse and industrial development, leaving the original two-mile oval largely demolished.

tracks.name: Barber Motorsports Park
tracks.summary: Immaculate, park-like road course near Birmingham, Alabama, adjoining a renowned motorcycle museum; an IndyCar venue.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Barber Motorsports Park opened in 2003 on rolling countryside east of Birmingham, in Leeds, Alabama. It was the creation of businessman George W. Barber, whose vintage-vehicle collection became the adjoining Barber Vintage Motorsports Museum, which houses more than 1,600 motorcycles and is recognised as one of the world's largest such collections. The road course was laid out by circuit designer Alan Wilson. Meticulous landscaping across the 880-acre park earned it the nickname "the Augusta National of motorsports."

## The circuit
The permanent road course runs 2.38 miles (3.83 km) through 17 turns and features roughly 80 feet (24 m) of elevation change. Its flowing, tree-lined layout blends fast sweeps with tighter technical corners, and a comparatively narrow racing surface places a premium on precision and track position. Sculptures and manicured grounds lend the venue an unusual park-like character. Beyond race weekends it operates as a driving school and manufacturer test facility, and it holds an FIA Grade 2 licence.

## Racing at Barber
The park is best known as an IndyCar venue, having hosted the Indy Grand Prix of Alabama since 2010 after the series first tested there in the late 2000s. The race has remained a fixture on the championship calendar, including in 2026, though its title sponsorship has changed over the years. Barber also stages national-level motorcycle and sports-car competition, having welcomed MotoAmerica superbike rounds and GT World Challenge America, and it hosts the annual Barber Vintage Festival, a large gathering of historic machines. Its elevation changes, rhythmic layout and limited passing zones tend to reward qualifying position and clean race strategy.

tracks.name: Bristol Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: Steeply banked half-mile 'bullring' in Tennessee known for its short-track intensity and colosseum-like grandstands.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Bristol Motor Speedway opened on 23 July 1961 in the hills of northeastern Tennessee, close to the Virginia border. It was originally called Bristol International Speedway, later Bristol International Raceway, before taking its present name in 1996, the year Speedway Motorsports acquired the track. Conceived as a compact, steeply banked oval, it was reshaped over the following decades into one of stock-car racing's most distinctive short tracks.

## The circuit
The half-mile oval measures 0.533 miles (0.858 km), with four turns banked at roughly 24 to 28 degrees that keep cars at near-constant high revolutions. Originally paved in asphalt, the racing surface was converted to concrete in 1992. Grandstands rise almost vertically around the full perimeter, seating around 146,000 spectators in their modern configuration and giving the venue its nickname, "the Last Great Colosseum." The short lap, steep banking and enclosed bowl amplify noise, speed and contact in the manner of a classic short-track bullring.

## Racing at Bristol
Bristol has hosted NASCAR Cup Series racing since 1961 and remains on the schedule, its calendar anchored by the spring Food City 500 and the late-summer Bass Pro Shops Night Race, run under floodlights. The tight confines make close contact and frequent cautions a defining feature, and the night race has grown into one of the sport's marquee dates. Between 2021 and 2023 the speedway covered its concrete with clay to stage dirt-surface Cup races, a nod to NASCAR's early history, before reverting to concrete for the 2024 season.

tracks.name: Charlotte Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: 1.5-mile North Carolina quad-oval that hosts the Coca-Cola 600; also runs a NASCAR event on its infield 'roval'.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Charlotte Motor Speedway opened on 15 June 1960 in Concord, North Carolina, just outside the city of Charlotte. It was founded by promoter Bruton Smith and driver Curtis Turner and became the cornerstone of what later grew into the Speedway Motorsports group. Among the earliest purpose-built superspeedways in stock-car racing, it staged its inaugural race, the World 600, that same year, establishing the long-distance tradition that still defines the venue.

## The circuit
The 1.5-mile (2.414 km) quad-oval carries four turns banked at 24 degrees, its distinctive four-cornered frontstretch giving spectators an extended view of the field. Alongside the oval, the facility includes an infield road course first used in 1971 and reconfigured in 2018 into a hybrid "roval" that links part of the banked oval to a twisting infield section. Permanent lighting allows night racing, and the intermediate oval rewards aerodynamic balance and sustained speed.

## Racing at Charlotte
Charlotte remains a NASCAR Cup Series venue with two events each year. The Coca-Cola 600, run on the oval over the Memorial Day weekend, is the longest race in NASCAR at 600 miles and ranks among the sport's "crown jewel" events; it descends directly from the 1960 World 600. From 2018 to 2025 the autumn playoff race was run on the "roval," a hybrid of the oval and infield road course that added right-hand corners and hard braking zones, before the event returned to the 1.5-mile oval in 2026. For many years the circuit also hosted the NASCAR All-Star Race, an exhibition event that has since rotated among other tracks. The speedway further serves as a hub of the stock-car industry, with numerous teams and suppliers based nearby.

tracks.name: Circuit of the Americas
tracks.summary: Purpose-built Austin circuit with a steep uphill Turn 1; hosts the United States Grand Prix and the Grand Prix of the Americas MotoGP round.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Circuit of the Americas opened on 21 October 2012 in southeastern Travis County, near Austin, Texas, as the first facility in the United States purpose-built for Formula One. The project was led by promoter Tavo Hellmund, with the layout designed by Hermann Tilke and shaped partly by input from motorcycle champion Kevin Schwantz. From the outset it was intended to host both car and motorcycle world championships.

## The circuit
The Grand Prix layout runs 3.426 miles (5.513 km) over 20 turns — more of them left-handers than right — and is driven anti-clockwise. Its signature feature is the approach to Turn 1, a blind, sharply uphill left-hander reached by a gradient of more than 11 per cent. Elsewhere the design deliberately evokes celebrated corners from other circuits, including a rapid esses sequence and a tighter stadium complex. The blend of gradient, heavy braking zones and fast, flowing curves tests aerodynamic efficiency and mechanical grip in equal measure. An observation tower and amphitheatre overlook the infield.

## Racing at COTA
The circuit has hosted the Formula One United States Grand Prix every year since 2012, apart from 2020, and it is contracted to remain on the calendar through 2034. Grand Prix motorcycle racing arrived in 2013, and COTA has since served as the United States round of the MotoGP World Championship, long promoted as the Grand Prix of the Americas. The venue has also hosted IndyCar, World Endurance Championship sports cars and NASCAR competition, making it one of the most versatile major racing sites in North America.

tracks.name: Darlington Raceway
tracks.summary: Egg-shaped South Carolina oval, 'the track too tough to tame', where drivers earn the 'Darlington stripe' on the wall.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Darlington Raceway opened on 19 August 1950 in Darlington, South Carolina, built by local businessman Harold Brasington, who set out to bring Indianapolis-style speedway racing to the Southeast. Its inaugural Southern 500 that year was NASCAR's first 500-mile race and the first held on a paved superspeedway. The track's unusual shape came from a construction compromise: to avoid disturbing a landowner's pond at one end, Brasington tightened those turns, producing the asymmetric oval that survives today.

## The circuit
The egg-shaped oval measures 1.366 miles (2.198 km) and has four turns, the first pair built to a wider radius than the second. That asymmetry forces drivers to adopt two different cornering techniques on a single lap and pushes cars perilously close to the outer wall on exit. Brushing that wall is so common that the resulting scrape is known as the "Darlington stripe." The difficulty of taming the layout produced the nicknames "the Lady in Black" and "the track too tough to tame."

## Racing at Darlington
Darlington has hosted NASCAR Cup Series racing since 1950 and remains on the schedule. Its centrepiece is the Southern 500, traditionally run over the Labor Day weekend and now presented as a throwback celebration of the sport's heritage, with teams and drivers adopting historic liveries and paint schemes; in recent seasons it has also opened the Cup Series playoffs. A second, spring Cup date returned in 2021 after a long absence. Owned by NASCAR itself since 2019, Darlington endures as one of the oldest and most challenging ovals in the championship.

tracks.name: Daytona International Speedway
tracks.summary: High-banked 2.5-mile tri-oval that hosts the Daytona 500 and, on its combined road course, the Rolex 24 sports-car race.
tracks.article:
## Origins

Daytona International Speedway opened in 1959, built by NASCAR founder Bill France Sr. to replace the stock-car racing that had been held on the beach and public road at Daytona Beach. Its high-banked design was intended to allow far higher speeds than a flat oval while improving the view for spectators.

## The circuit

The main oval is 2.5 miles (4.02 km) long, with 31 degrees of banking in the turns, and introduced the "tri-oval" shape — a shallow kink on the pit straight that improved sightlines. The steep banking and long straights make Daytona a superspeedway, where cars run in tightly packed drafting formations at sustained high speed. An infield road course combines with the banking to form a 3.56-mile circuit used for sports-car racing.

## Racing at Daytona

The circuit's signature event is the Daytona 500. Unusually, NASCAR opens its season with its most prestigious race, and a win in the "Great American Race" can define a driver's career. On the road course, the Rolex 24 at Daytona has been staged since 1966 and is one of the world's major endurance events, opening the international sports-car season each January. A redevelopment between 2013 and 2016 rebuilt the grandstands around roughly 101,500 seats, reaffirming Daytona's standing as one of the most famous venues in American motorsport.

tracks.name: Detroit Street Circuit
tracks.summary: A tight downtown street circuit in Detroit, Michigan that hosted the United States Grand Prix from 1982 to 1988. (Later Detroit races moved to Belle Isle, and from 2023 to a separate downtown IndyCar circuit.)
tracks.article:
## Origins
The Detroit Street Circuit was laid out through the streets of downtown Detroit and opened on 4 June 1982, when the city first staged the Detroit Grand Prix, one of the United States rounds of the Formula One World Championship. Civic promoters pursued the event to raise the city's profile, and the course was built around the Renaissance Center and Cobo Arena beside the Detroit River, taking in part of Woodward Avenue. It joined Long Beach and the Caesars Palace race at Las Vegas among the American grands prix of the early 1980s.

## The circuit
The temporary layout was tight, flat and lined with concrete barriers, threading between office towers and hotels with little run-off. Its settled configuration, used from 1983, measured 2.5 miles (4.023 km) and packed in 22 corners; the 1982 debut had run a marginally longer 2.59-mile course of 24 turns. The surface was notoriously bumpy and low on grip, and the confined pit and paddock area drew persistent criticism. Low average speeds placed a premium on traction, braking stability and mechanical precision rather than outright power.

## Racing at Detroit
The circuit hosted the Detroit Grand Prix each year from 1982 to 1988. John Watson produced one of the era's celebrated drives at the 1982 event, winning for McLaren from 17th on the grid, while Ayrton Senna took three consecutive victories from 1986 to 1988. After the 1988 race, the sport's governing body judged the pit and paddock facilities inadequate for a world championship event, and Formula One left. CART Indy car racing continued on the downtown streets from 1989 to 1991 before the Detroit Grand Prix relocated to Belle Isle in 1992. A reconfigured downtown circuit, separate from this original course, has hosted IndyCar racing since 2023.

tracks.name: Dover Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: High-banked concrete one-mile Delaware oval nicknamed the 'Monster Mile'.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Dover Motor Speedway opened in 1969 near Dover, Delaware, as a combined horse- and auto-racing facility. It began life as Dover Downs International Speedway, was renamed Dover International Speedway in 2002, and took its current name in 2021. NASCAR's premier stock-car division has raced on the one-mile oval since its opening season. Built originally in asphalt, the track was resurfaced in concrete in 1995, an unusual material that has shaped both its racing character and its identity.

## The circuit
The oval measures exactly one mile (1.609 km), with four turns banked at 24 degrees and the straights at nine degrees, steep figures for so short a track. The concrete surface, high banking and tight dimensions generate heavy tyre wear, high g-loadings and a jarring ride that gave the venue its nickname, the "Monster Mile." A single preferred groove through the corners makes clean passing difficult and contact common, and cars are back into a turn almost as soon as they have cleared the last. A 46-foot statue, "Miles the Monster," installed in 2008, overlooks the grounds.

## Racing at Dover
Dover held at least one NASCAR Cup Series points race in every season from 1969, building a reputation as one of the schedule's most punishing tests; it also stages Xfinity Series and Craftsman Truck Series events. For 2026 the track took on the NASCAR All-Star Race, the sport's midseason exhibition, in a swap that moved its Cup points date to North Wilkesboro Speedway and ended its unbroken run of championship points races. Speedway Motorsports acquired the facility in December 2021.

tracks.name: Trackhouse Motorplex (formerly GoPro Motorplex)
tracks.summary: America's premier outdoor kart track at Mooresville, North Carolina, its layout inspired by Italy's Parma circuit.

tracks.name: Homestead-Miami Speedway
tracks.summary: A 1.5-mile oval in Homestead, Florida, whose progressive banking produces wide, multi-groove racing. It hosted NASCAR's season finale from 2002 to 2019, and the Cup Series championship finale is set to return there in 2026 under a new rotating model.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Homestead-Miami Speedway opened in November 1995 in Homestead, Florida. The promoter Ralph Sanchez advanced the project as part of southern Miami-Dade County's recovery from Hurricane Andrew, which had struck the region in 1992. The track first ran as a flat, rectangular quad-oval; it was reshaped into a true oval in 1997 and gained its current variable, progressive banking in a 2003 reconfiguration, each change intended to improve the quality of stock-car racing.

## The circuit
The oval measures 1.5 miles (2.414 km) and has four turns. Its defining feature is progressive banking that varies from 18 to 20 degrees through the corners, with the straights banked at four degrees. The design lets drivers work several lines, from the flatter bottom of the track to the higher, faster lane against the outside wall, while the abrasive surface wears tyres heavily over a fuel run. Those traits have made Homestead a circuit that rewards tyre management and patience, especially in the closing laps of longer races.

## Racing at Homestead
Homestead hosted the season-ending finale for NASCAR's Cup, Xfinity and Truck series from 2002 to 2019, staging many of the era's title deciders, before championship weekend moved to Phoenix Raceway for 2020. Under a new model that rotates the finale among NASCAR's marquee venues, championship weekend returns to Homestead in 2026, with the Cup Series title race set for 8 November. The venue also hosted top-level open-wheel racing: CART's Grand Prix of Miami ran from 1996 to 2000, and the Indy Racing League and later IndyCar competed there from 2001 until 2010.

tracks.name: Indianapolis Motor Speedway
tracks.summary: The 2.5-mile 'Brickyard', home of the Indianapolis 500; its infield road course hosted the United States Grand Prix from 2000 to 2007.
tracks.article:
## Origins
Indianapolis Motor Speedway opened on 14 August 1909 in Speedway, Indiana. Its original surface of crushed stone and tar broke up dangerously, and later in 1909 the owners repaved the 2.5-mile oval with 3.2 million paving bricks, giving rise to the enduring nickname "the Brickyard." The bricks were later covered with asphalt, but a one-yard-wide strip remains exposed at the start-finish line, where winners traditionally kiss the bricks.

## The circuit
The rectangular oval measures 2.5 miles (4.023 km) and comprises four turns banked at 9.2 degrees, linked by two long straights and two shorter chutes. Its dimensions have remained essentially unchanged since 1909, making it one of the oldest major circuits in continuous operation.
